title: The Stock Market Explained With One Lemonade Stand

beats.text: When you buy a share of Apple, Apple doesn't get a single cent of your money.
So who does? And if the company doesn't get the money, why does the stock market even exist?
To answer that, we only need one thing. A lemonade stand.
Meet Penny. Penny sells lemonade. A cup sells for a dollar, and costs about forty cents to make.
On a good summer, she sells a thousand cups. That's six hundred dollars of profit.
Penny wants a second stand, across town. That needs a thousand dollars she doesn't have.
She could borrow it. But a loan has to be paid back, with interest, even if it rains all summer.
So she has another idea.
She splits her business into one hundred equal slices. These slices are called shares.
Each share is one percent of the stand. One percent of the cups, the profits, and the future.
She keeps sixty shares, and sells forty to her neighbours, for twenty-five dollars each.
Penny gets her thousand dollars. She builds the second stand. And her neighbours now own part of her business.
Grandma bought ten shares. With two stands, the business now makes twelve hundred dollars a year. Ten percent of that belongs to Grandma.
Some of the profit, Penny keeps to grow. Some, she pays out to her shareholders. That payout is called a dividend.
This is exactly what Apple did in nineteen eighty. It sold shares to the public for the first time. That's called an I. P. O., an initial public offering.
Apple sold shares at twenty-two dollars each, and raised about a hundred million dollars.
That first sale is when the company gets the money. And it's almost the only time it does.
Because now, Grandma wants a new bicycle. She doesn't want to own lemonade any more. She wants cash.
She can't make Penny buy her shares back. But she can sell them to someone else. Sam, next door, offers thirty dollars a share.
Grandma gets three hundred dollars. Sam gets ten shares. And Penny? Penny gets nothing. The money went from Sam, to Grandma.
That's the stock market. Not a place where companies get money, but a place where owners trade with each other.
When you buy Apple shares today, you're buying them from another investor who wanted to sell. Apple isn't involved.
So, the answer to our question. Your money goes to whoever sold you the share.
So why does the price matter to Penny at all?
Because the price is the town's vote on what her business is worth. A hundred shares at thirty dollars means the whole stand is worth three thousand.
That's called market capitalisation. And a high price helps Penny. Next time she needs money, she can sell new shares for more.
So what moves the price? Just two things. How many people want to buy, and how many want to sell.
A heatwave is forecast. Everyone expects record sales. Buyers rush in. Thirty dollars becomes fifty.
Then a rumour says a big chain is opening a juice bar on the same street. Sellers rush out. Fifty becomes twenty.
Nothing about the lemons changed. Only what people expect about the future.
Then it gets strange.
Word spreads that lemonade shares only ever go up. People start buying, not for the lemonade, but because they expect to sell to someone else for more.
The price hits a thousand dollars a share. A business making twelve hundred dollars a year, priced at a hundred thousand.
It would take more than eighty years of profits to earn that back. That's a bubble.
Not everyone is fooled. A trader called Rex thinks the price is crazy.
He borrows ten shares from Sam, and promises to give ten shares back later. Then he sells them, right away, for a thousand dollars each.
If the price crashes, he can buy ten shares back cheap, return them to Sam, and keep the difference. That's short selling.
It's a bet that the price will fall. And it's dangerous. If the price keeps rising, his losses have no limit.
Then autumn arrives. Sales slow. Somebody sells. Then everybody sells.
A thousand dollars. Five hundred. A hundred. Forty.
Rex buys back ten shares at forty dollars, hands them back to Sam, and keeps nine thousand six hundred dollars.
The people who bought at the top have lost almost everything, on paper.
And Penny's lemonade? It tastes exactly the same. Two stands. Twelve hundred dollars a year. The business never changed. Only the price did.
That's the whole stock market. A company sells slices of itself once, to raise money. After that, the owners trade the slices with each other.
The price is just the latest deal between a buyer and a seller. It's what people expect, not what the business is.
So when you buy a share of Apple, you're not giving Apple money.
You're buying a slice of its future, from someone who'd rather have the cash.
